catalog_quote: Most conspicuous among the many developments which characterize Northern Paman reflection of Proto Paman is the reduction of Initial syllables (*CV1) by loss of initial consonants (*C1) and loss or other reduction of immediately following vowels (*V1). Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems. In all Northern Paman languages, except Uraði and its sister dialects, *C1 was lost invariably. Even in Uraði the prevailing tendency has been toward initial loss, although *C1 is sometimes positively reflected in that language. Short *V1 was lost in some languages, retained in others, and metathesized in still others. Long *V·1 was shortened in all. ... [p. 179, of Linngithigh only] Word stress in Linŋit̯iɣ is predictable: the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed. Accordingly, the first vowel is stressed in words beginning in a consonant or cluster -- kápan short, ŋgóðRo black -- but the second vowel in words which begin in a vowel -- ayóŋ I, alán sky, aðá crow.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement only: in Hale's account the Northern Paman languages (his 1960 sample includes Mpalityan and Lutiɣ, pp. 163-164) shifted primary stress from the first to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem, after which the initial consonant, and often the initial vowel, was lost. Synchronically this puts stress on the first vowel that is preceded by a consonant: initial in consonant-initial words, second syllable in vowel-initial words. Hale states that synchronic rule explicitly only for Linngithigh (p. 179) and, in Hale 1976b (snippet), calls it 'apparently shared by all of the Northern Paman languages'. No opened source or snippet gives a Mpalitjanh- or Luthigh-specific stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Uradhi and its sister dialects did not lose *C1 invariably. Crowley 1983 (held by the project) gives Uradhi a different rule (antepenultimate; long vowels attract stress), so the 'shared by all Northern Paman' rule is not universal in the subgroup and its application to Mpalitjanh-Luthigh is an inference.
new_statements.domain_note: Diachronic statement about Paman stems (word level); stress called 'a strictly phonetic feature', i.e. non-contrastive. Applies to Mpalitjanh-Luthigh only by membership in 'all Northern Paman languages'; the language's own entry (p. 164) and the 1976a snippets are silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog language mpal1237 'Mpalityanh-Luthigh' = Hale's 'Mpalityan and Lutiɣ', 'two closely related dialects.. spoken in the middle and upper Ducie River area' (Hale 1966: 164); dialects Mpalitjanh mpal1238 [xpj] (AIATSIS Y25; = McConnel's Lɔ:tig) and Luthigh luth1234 (AIATSIS Y12; = McConnel's Tepiti). The quoted statement is Hale's Northern Paman group statement, not a description of either dialect; the same sentence has been used by sibling checks for Ngkoth (ngko1236), Mbiywom (mbiy1238), Alngith (alng1239) etc., so it should not be counted as an independent description for each. Reviewer should treat this as a group-level inference (fixed: other position: initial in C-initial words, second syllable in V-initial words), confidence low.

new_statements.relation_note: The stress sentence is word-for-word the passage already recorded from Hale 1966 (AL 8(2): 167-168) and confirms Blevins 2001's citation of Hale 1964: 256 for it. It supports the catalog's fixed: other position, group-level reading (stress shifted off the initial syllable in all Northern Paman languages including Mpalityan and Lutiɣ) and adds no Mpalityan- or Lutiɣ-specific stress information; it is compatible with, but does not itself state, the synchronic 'first vowel after a consonant' rule. It does not support the catalog record's 'segmental' kind with an empty rule; the compilers fixed: other position stands.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level, diachronic only: in the Northern Paman languages (of which Mpalityan and Lutiɣ are sample (B), p. 252) primary stress shifted from the first to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem, and this shift drove the loss of the initial consonant and reduction of the first vowel. No synchronic rule is stated for any language; the closest synchronic equivalent (stress the first post-consonantal vowel: initial syllable in C-initial words, second syllable in V-initial words) appears only in Hale 1966 (for Linngithigh) and Hale 1976b (Uradhi, 'apparently shared by all of the Northern Paman languages').
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. The only exception clause in the passage concerns initial-consonant loss, not stress: Uraði and its sister dialects sometimes retain *C1 (p. 256). The paper's Mpalityan/Lutiɣ-specific remarks concern segments only: p. 259 'In Yinwum and in Mpalityan, *NS lost the nasal segment itself, but the stop remained as prenasalized'; p. 260 'In Mpalityan and Lutiɣ, *V1 was sometimes lost, sometimes retained, and sometimes metathesized.'
new_statements.identity_note: Hale 1964 p. 252 lists '(B) Mpalityan, Lutiɣ' as one of eight Northern Paman subgroups among the 13 samples recorded in 1960 at Weipa and Aurukun Missions; pp. 252-253: 'These two closely related dialects were spoken in the middle and upper Ducie River area', Mpalityan corresponding to McConnel's (1950) Lɔ:tig north of the Ducie and Lutiɣ to her Tepiti south of the Ducie. This matches Glottolog mpal1237 (Mpalitjanh [xpj] + Luthigh). The stress statement itself is made for Northern Paman as a whole (all 13 varieties), not for this pair specifically.
